title: Implement AI Risk Management and Assessments
intro: How to identify, quantify and map AI risks; run impact assessments that cover people, blast radius and autonomous actions; tier use cases by human impact and technical complexity; choose risk treatments and accept residual risk properly; and define the triggers that force a fresh assessment.
objectives: Categorise AI risks and analyse them qualitatively and quantitatively, including SLE, ARO, ALE and safeguard value
Write risk register entries and map risks to system components, lifecycle stages and threat catalogues
Run impact assessments (DPIA, FRIA, AI system and algorithmic) and analyse blast radius and autonomous actions
Design a risk-tiering model based on human impact and technical complexity, with proportionate requirements
Select avoid, mitigate, transfer or accept treatments and formally accept residual risk
Define reassessment triggers and connect them to change, monitoring and threat-intelligence processes

sections.title: Identifying, quantifying and mapping AI risk

scenes.title: Putting numbers on AI risk
scenes.sub: Risk categories, qualitative and quantitative analysis, and the risk register
scenes.say: Risk management turns worry into decisions. To do that for AI, you need to know what can go wrong, how likely it is, and how much it would hurt. | This video covers AI risk categories, qualitative and quantitative analysis, and how risks are recorded and mapped.

scenes.title: Categories of AI risk

items.d: Attacks on models, data, prompts and tools
Leakage, inference and unlawful processing
Discriminatory or exclusionary outcomes
Errors, hallucinations, unsafe actions, drift
Regulatory breaches, IP infringement, liability
Outages, vendor changes, cost overruns

scenes.say: AI risks fall into a handful of categories, and a good assessment considers them all. | Security: attacks on models, training data, prompts and connected tools. | Privacy: leakage of personal data, inferences about people, and unlawful processing. | Fairness: discriminatory or exclusionary outcomes. | Reliability and safety: errors, hallucinations, unsafe actions and drift. | Legal and compliance: regulatory breaches, intellectual property infringement and liability. | And operational and third-party risk: outages, silent vendor changes and cost overruns. Each can also cause reputational damage.

scenes.title: Two ways to analyse risk
rows: Rate likelihood and impact on scales such as low to high
Estimate frequency and loss in money
Fast; works without much data; easy to communicate
Subjective; hard to compare or aggregate
Needs data that is scarce for new AI risks
scenes.say: There are two broad ways to analyse risk. | Qualitative analysis rates likelihood and impact on scales, such as low, medium and high. Quantitative analysis estimates how often a loss will happen, and how much it will cost, in money. | Qualitative analysis is fast, works without much data, and is easy to communicate. Quantitative analysis supports cost-benefit decisions, such as whether a control is worth its price. | But qualitative ratings are subjective and hard to aggregate, while quantitative estimates need data that is often scarce for new AI risks. Most organisations use both.

scenes.title: A heat map of AI risks
scenes.say: A heat map plots each risk by likelihood and impact, so the most urgent stand out. Here is an assessment for an external customer assistant. | Prompt injection through customer messages is likely, with moderate impact. | Minor hallucinations are likely, but with limited impact because answers are grounded and reviewed. | Biased handling of complaints is possible, with severe impact on people. | So is leakage of customer data through the assistant. | And theft of the model is rare, but severe. The top-right cells demand action first.

scenes.def: SLE = asset value × exposure factor = £2m × 20% = £400,000. ALE = SLE × ARO = £400,000 × 0.25 = £100,000.
scenes.ex: A control costing £30,000 a year that cuts ARO to 0.05 saves £80,000 in ALE: worth £50,000 a year.
scenes.say: Here is the classic quantitative formula. Annualised loss expectancy is the expected loss per year from one risk scenario. | First, the single loss expectancy: the asset value multiplied by the exposure factor, the share of value lost in one event. Two million pounds at twenty per cent is four hundred thousand. Multiply by the annualised rate of occurrence, here once every four years, or point two five, and the ALE is one hundred thousand pounds a year. | Now a control costing thirty thousand a year that cuts the rate to point oh five lowers the ALE to twenty thousand, an eighty thousand pound reduction. Subtract its cost, and the control is worth fifty thousand pounds a year.

scenes.title: Writing a good risk register entry

items.d: Cause, event and consequence, in one sentence
A named person with authority to act
Before and after controls
Existing controls, planned actions, deadlines
Signals that the risk is rising

scenes.say: Each risk is recorded in a register. | Start with a clear risk statement: cause, event and consequence. For example: because the assistant reads customer emails, an attacker could embed instructions that cause it to disclose another customer’s data, leading to a reportable breach. | Give it a named owner with authority to act. | Record the inherent rating, before controls, and the residual rating, after them. | List existing controls and the treatment plan, with deadlines. | And define key risk indicators, such as the rate of blocked injection attempts, that warn you when the risk is rising.

items: Consider security, privacy, fairness, reliability, legal, operational
Qualitative for speed; quantitative for cost–benefit
ALE = SLE × ARO; SLE = asset value × exposure factor
Register: statement, owner, ratings, controls, KRIs
scenes.say: To recap. | Consider every category of AI risk: security, privacy, fairness, reliability and safety, legal and operational. | Use qualitative analysis for speed and communication, and quantitative analysis to justify spending. | Annualised loss expectancy equals single loss expectancy times the annualised rate of occurrence. | And a good register entry has a clear statement, an owner, inherent and residual ratings, controls and key risk indicators.

blocks.md:
### What makes AI risk different
AI risk management uses the same foundations as any risk management, as described in ISO 31000 and applied to AI in ISO/IEC 23894 and the NIST AI RMF. But several features of AI make it harder:

- **Harms to others.** Many AI harms fall on people outside the organisation, such as applicants, patients and the public, so impact must be assessed for individuals, groups and society, not only the organisation.
- **Limited loss data.** New attack techniques and failure modes have little history, so frequency estimates are uncertain.
- **Non-determinism and emergence.** Systems can behave differently on similar inputs, and capabilities can surprise their builders.
- **Dependency chains.** Models, datasets, libraries and APIs from third parties introduce risks you don’t directly control.
- **Change.** Drift and model updates mean today’s rating can be wrong next quarter.

### Risk vocabulary
| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Risk** | The effect of uncertainty on objectives; commonly expressed as a combination of **likelihood** and **impact** |
| **Inherent risk** | Risk before considering controls |
| **Residual risk** | Risk remaining after controls |
| **Risk appetite** | The amount and type of risk an organisation is willing to pursue or retain in pursuit of its objectives |
| **Risk tolerance** | The acceptable variation around objectives; often expressed as thresholds for specific risks |
| **Key risk indicator (KRI)** | A metric that signals rising exposure, such as drift scores, injection attempts or complaint rates |

### Qualitative, semi-quantitative and quantitative analysis
- **Qualitative:** likelihood and impact on descriptive scales (for example, rare to almost certain; minor to severe), plotted on a heat map. Quick and accessible, but subjective.
- **Semi-quantitative:** numbers assigned to the scales (for example, 1–5 each, multiplied to give 1–25). Easy to rank, but the arithmetic can imply false precision.
- **Quantitative:** frequency and monetary loss. The classic formulas are:
  - **Single loss expectancy (SLE)** = asset value (AV) × exposure factor (EF)
  - **Annualised loss expectancy (ALE)** = SLE × annualised rate of occurrence (ARO)
  - **Value of a safeguard** = ALE before − ALE after − annual cost of the safeguard

**FAIR** (Factor Analysis of Information Risk) is a widely used quantitative model that decomposes risk into **loss event frequency** (threat event frequency × vulnerability) and **loss magnitude** (primary and secondary losses), usually estimated as ranges and simulated with Monte Carlo methods. Ranges are more honest than single numbers when data is scarce.

For AI, combine approaches: quantify financial exposure where you can (breach costs, fraud losses, fines, outages), and assess **impact on people** qualitatively, because harms such as discrimination or loss of autonomy don’t reduce neatly to money.

### Mapping AI risks
Risk **mapping** connects each risk to where it arises and how it is tracked:
1. **To the system:** which component creates the exposure (training data, model, prompts and retrieval, tools and agents, outputs, infrastructure, suppliers).
2. **To the lifecycle:** design, data collection, training, evaluation, deployment, operation, retirement.
3. **To threat and risk catalogues:** MITRE ATLAS techniques, the OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications, the NIST Generative AI Profile’s twelve risks, and repositories such as the MIT AI Risk Repository, so that nothing obvious is missed and findings use common language.
4. **To controls and owners:** each risk links to the controls that treat it and the person accountable for it.

This mapping lets you answer questions such as “which of our systems are exposed to indirect prompt injection, and who owns each?” and supports the NIST AI RMF **Map** function.

blocks.title: Work an ALE example
items: Define the scenario

An AI support assistant could leak customer records through indirect prompt injection. The records are valued at £2,000,000 (cost of notification, remediation, fines and lost business if all were exposed).
Estimate the exposure factor
A realistic incident would expose about 20% of records: EF = 0.2.
Calculate SLE
Estimate ARO
Given current controls and threat activity, such an incident is expected about once every four years: ARO = 0.25.
Calculate ALE
Evaluate a control

Isolating retrieved content and requiring approval for data exports costs £30,000 a year and cuts ARO to 0.05. New ALE = £20,000. Value = £100,000 − £20,000 − £30,000 = £50,000 per year, so the control is justified.

blocks.title: Formula traps
blocks.md:
- **SLE = AV × EF**, not AV × ARO.
- **ALE = SLE × ARO**. An ARO of 0.25 means once every four years; an ARO of 4 means four times a year.
- A safeguard is worth buying when **ALE reduction > its annual cost**. Never spend more on a control than the loss it prevents, unless law or ethics requires it.

q.q: A model-theft scenario has an asset value of £5 million, an exposure factor of 40% and an expected occurrence of once every ten years. What is the ALE?

blocks.title: Who could this hurt, and how badly?

scenes.title: Who could this hurt, and how badly?
scenes.sub: Impact assessments, blast radius and autonomous actions
scenes.say: Risk assessment asks what could go wrong for the organisation. Impact assessment asks what could go wrong for people, and how far the damage could spread. | This video covers the main types of impact assessment, blast-radius analysis, and how to assess AI that acts on its own.

scenes.title: Four kinds of impact assessment

items.d: GDPR: high-risk processing of personal data
EU AI Act: certain deployers of high-risk AI
ISO/IEC 42001 and 42005: individuals, groups and society
Public-sector tools that score impact and set required measures

scenes.say: You will meet four main kinds of impact assessment, and they overlap. | A data protection impact assessment is required by the GDPR before processing personal data in ways likely to be high risk, which covers many AI uses. | A fundamental rights impact assessment is required by the EU AI Act for public bodies and certain private deployers, such as credit and insurance providers, before using high-risk AI. | An AI system impact assessment, required by ISO forty-two thousand and one and described in ISO forty-two thousand and five, looks at consequences for individuals, groups and society across the life cycle. | And algorithmic impact assessments, used by governments such as Canada’s, score a system’s impact level and set the safeguards each level requires. A single well-designed assessment can satisfy several of these at once.

scenes.title: What a good assessment covers

items.d: What it does, where, and for whom
Users and non-users; vulnerable groups
Physical, financial, psychological, rights, societal
Including scale and reversibility
Controls, human review, redress
Residual impact, sign-off, next review

scenes.say: Whatever its name, a good assessment covers six things. | Purpose and context: what the system does, where, and for whom. | Affected people: users and non-users alike, with attention to vulnerable groups. | Potential harms: physical, financial, psychological, harms to rights such as privacy and non-discrimination, and wider societal harms. | Severity and likelihood, including how many people could be affected and whether the harm can be reversed. | Mitigations and oversight, including human review and routes to redress. | And the decision: the residual impact, who signed it off, and when it will be reviewed.

scenes.title: Blast radius: how far could it spread?

note.text: Shrink the radius: scope, isolate, limit, approve.

scenes.say: Blast radius is a security idea: if this system misbehaves or is compromised, everything it can reach is in the zone of damage. Imagine a customer-service agent manipulated by text hidden in an email it reads. | It can send email as the company and read and export customer records, so it could run a phishing campaign or leak data. | It can approve refunds and change files, so it could move money or destroy records. | And it can delegate to other agents, spreading the problem further. | The blast radius is defined by the agent’s permissions and connections, not by its intended purpose. Reduce it with least privilege, isolation, limits on value and volume, and approval for high-impact actions.

scenes.title: Assessing autonomous actions

items.d: Every tool, permission and connected system
Speed and scale multiply the damage
Irreversible actions need stronger controls
Monitoring, alerts and human oversight
Kill switch, revocation and safe fallback

scenes.say: For AI that acts, the assessment asks five extra questions. | What can it do? List every tool, permission and connected system, because that is the blast radius. | How fast and how often? An agent that acts thousands of times an hour can cause harm faster than any person can notice. | Can its actions be undone? Payments, deletions and messages sent externally usually can’t, so they need approval or strict limits. | Who would notice when it goes wrong? Define the monitoring and alerts that would catch misbehaviour. | And can it be stopped? There must be a tested way to halt it, revoke its credentials and fall back safely.

items: DPIA, FRIA, AI system and algorithmic impact assessments overlap
Cover people, harms, severity, mitigations and sign-off
Blast radius = everything a system can reach
Autonomy: scope, speed, reversibility, detection, stopping
scenes.say: To recap. | DPIAs, fundamental rights impact assessments, AI system impact assessments and algorithmic impact assessments overlap, so design one process that satisfies them all. | Cover affected people, harms, severity, mitigations and a documented decision. | Blast radius is everything a system can reach if it misbehaves. | And for autonomous systems, assess scope, speed, reversibility, detection and the ability to stop them.

blocks.md:
### Impact assessment versus risk assessment
A **risk assessment** typically asks how uncertainty affects the *organisation’s* objectives. An **impact assessment** asks how a system could affect *people, groups and society*. ISO/IEC 42001 requires both: an AI risk assessment (clause 6.1.2) and an AI system impact assessment (clause 6.1.4). In practice the impact assessment feeds the risk assessment: severe impacts on people become legal, reputational and ethical risks for the organisation.

### The main assessment types
| Assessment | Source | When required | Focus |
|---|---|---|---|
| **DPIA** | GDPR Article 35 | Before processing likely to result in high risk to individuals (for example, systematic profiling, large-scale special-category data, innovative technology) | Necessity, proportionality, risks to data subjects, mitigating measures; prior consultation with the regulator if high risk remains (Article 36) |
| **FRIA** | EU AI Act Article 27 | Before deploying high-risk AI, for public bodies, private entities providing public services, and deployers assessing creditworthiness or pricing life and health insurance | Deployer’s processes, affected categories of people, specific risks of harm, human oversight, measures if risks materialise; results notified to the market surveillance authority; can build on a DPIA |
| **AI system impact assessment** | ISO/IEC 42001 (6.1.4); guidance in ISO/IEC 42005:2025 | For AI systems within the AIMS scope, across the lifecycle | Consequences for individuals, groups and society, including foreseeable misuse; documented and used in risk treatment |
| **Algorithmic impact assessment** | Public-sector policies, such as Canada’s Directive on Automated Decision-Making | Before government automated decision systems are used | A questionnaire produces an impact level (I to IV), each with mandatory measures such as peer review, notice, human involvement and explanation |

### Running an impact assessment
1. **Describe** the system: purpose, context, data, model, outputs, decisions influenced, degree of autonomy.
2. **Identify stakeholders:** users, people subject to decisions, bystanders, and **vulnerable groups** such as children, people with disabilities or people in financial difficulty.
3. **Identify potential harms and benefits:** physical, psychological, financial, harms to rights (privacy, non-discrimination, freedom of expression, due process), and societal or environmental harms. Include **foreseeable misuse**, not only intended use.
4. **Assess severity and likelihood,** considering scale (how many people), reversibility, and whether harm falls disproportionately on some groups.
5. **Define mitigations:** design changes, controls, human oversight, transparency, redress mechanisms.
6. **Decide and document:** residual impact, who accepted it, conditions, and the review date.
7. **Revisit** on change and periodically.

Involving **affected stakeholders** (or their representatives) improves assessments significantly; people who live with the consequences notice harms that designers miss.

### Blast radius
In security, **blast radius** is the extent of damage if a component fails or is compromised. For AI, it is determined by:
- **Data reach:** what information the system can read, and therefore leak.
- **Action reach:** what it can change, send, buy, delete or approve.
- **Connection reach:** which other systems, agents and users its outputs flow into.
- **Scale:** how many users, records or transactions it touches, and how quickly.

The radius depends on **permissions and integrations, not intentions**. An assistant designed to answer questions but connected with a broad service account has the blast radius of that account. Reducing blast radius is one of the most effective treatments: least-privilege credentials, segmentation, per-action limits, approval gates, and the ability to revoke access instantly.

### Assessing autonomous actions
Autonomy changes the impact profile. For agentic systems, assess:
- the **actions** available and the **authority** under which they run (the user’s, a service account’s, or delegated);
- **speed and volume**, since automated actions can cause harm faster than humans can respond;
- **reversibility** of each action;
- **detection**: how misbehaviour would be noticed, and how quickly;
- **interruption**: kill switches, credential revocation, rollback and safe fallback modes;
- **delegation**: whether the agent can hand tasks to other agents, extending the radius.

The output of this assessment drives the operational mode (Module 1.3) and the agent controls covered in Domain 4.

blocks.title: Three systems, three impact profiles
items: Internal meeting summariser

**Affected people:** meeting participants. **Main harms:** inaccurate summaries; sensitive discussions stored longer than expected. **Blast radius:** read-only access to meeting recordings for invited users. **Outcome:** low impact; standard DPIA screening, retention limits, and a notice to participants.
Tenant screening model

**Affected people:** rental applicants, including vulnerable groups. **Main harms:** discriminatory refusals; inaccurate data leading to wrongful rejection; lack of explanation. **Blast radius:** influences housing decisions for thousands of applicants. **Outcome:** high impact; full impact assessment and DPIA, bias testing, explanations, human review of refusals, appeal route.
IT operations agent

**Affected people:** all staff relying on IT services. **Main harms:** outages from wrong configuration changes; security exposure. **Blast radius:** administrative access to cloud infrastructure. **Outcome:** high operational impact; scoped credentials, change approval for production, rate limits, rollback, and a kill switch.

blocks.title: One assessment, several obligations
blocks.md: When a scenario mentions **GDPR, the AI Act and ISO/IEC 42001** together, the efficient answer is usually an **integrated impact assessment** that covers data protection, fundamental rights and broader societal impacts, rather than separate, disconnected documents. The AI Act itself allows a FRIA to build on an existing DPIA.

q.q: An AI assistant intended only to answer staff questions is connected to an administrator account with write access to the HR system. How should its blast radius be assessed?
o: By its intended purpose of answering staff questions, which makes the blast radius small
By the permissions and connections it actually has, including everything the admin account can change
By the number of questions it answers per day, which determines how many staff members it could affect in total
By the accuracy of its answers in testing, since wrong answers are the main way it could cause harm
q.why: Blast radius is defined by reach, not intent. A compromised or manipulated assistant can do anything its credentials allow, so least-privilege access is the key treatment.

scenes.title: Not every chatbot is a crisis
scenes.sub: Tiering AI use cases by human impact and technical complexity
scenes.say: If every AI use case gets the full assessment treatment, governance becomes a bottleneck and people route around it. If none do, harm slips through. | Risk tiers solve this, by matching the depth of scrutiny to the size of the risk. This video shows how to build them.

scenes.title: Two dimensions, four tiers

notes.d: How much the system can affect people’s rights, safety, money or opportunities.
How hard the system is to predict, control and secure: autonomy, opacity, untrusted inputs.
Higher tiers need deeper assessment, more oversight and senior approval.

scenes.say: A practical approach rates each use case on two dimensions. The first is human impact: how much the system can affect people’s rights, safety, finances or opportunities. | The second is technical complexity: how hard the system is to predict, control and secure, including its autonomy, opacity and exposure to untrusted inputs. | Combining them gives a tier. A simple, low-impact tool is tier one. A complex, high-impact system, such as an agent that makes decisions about people, is tier four. And the tier decides how much assessment, oversight and approval the use case needs.

scenes.title: Rating human impact

items.d: Jobs, credit, housing, benefits, healthcare
Physical harm or critical services
How many people; children or vulnerable groups
Can errors be noticed and undone?
Health, biometrics, finances, children
Customer-facing or public outputs

scenes.say: Human impact is rated on factors like these. | Does the system make or influence decisions about people, such as jobs, credit, housing, benefits or healthcare? | Could it cause physical harm, or disrupt critical services? | How many people does it affect, and are any of them children or otherwise vulnerable? | Can errors be noticed and reversed? | Does it process sensitive data, such as health, biometric or financial information? | And are its outputs visible to customers or the public?

scenes.title: Rating technical complexity

items.d: Does it act, or only suggest?
Can its behaviour be explained and predicted?
Web content, emails, uploads, external RAG sources
How many systems it can reach
Hosted models, plugins, opaque training data
New techniques with little operational history

scenes.say: Technical complexity has its own factors. | Autonomy and tool access: does the system act, or only suggest? | Opacity: can its behaviour be explained and predicted? | Untrusted inputs: does it process web content, emails, uploaded files or external documents that an attacker could influence? | Integration depth: how many other systems can it reach? | Third-party dependence: does it rely on hosted models, plugins or training data you can’t inspect? | And novelty: is it built on new techniques with little operational history?

scenes.title: What each tier requires (example)

layers.label: Tier 4: critical
layers.sub: Committee approval, full assessments, red team, HITL, continuous monitoring

layers.label: Tier 3: high
layers.sub: Impact assessment, bias and security testing, defined oversight, quarterly review

layers.label: Tier 2: moderate
layers.sub: Standard risk assessment, security review, owner sign-off, six-monthly review

layers.label: Tier 1: low
layers.sub: Checklist, approved tools only, manager approval, annual review

scenes.say: Each tier carries a defined set of requirements. Here is an example. | Tier four, critical: approval by the governance committee, the full set of impact, privacy and security assessments, red teaming, a human in the loop, and continuous monitoring. | Tier three, high: an impact assessment, bias and security testing, a defined oversight model and quarterly review. | Tier two, moderate: a standard risk assessment, a security review, sign-off by the business owner, and review every six months. | Tier one, low: a short checklist, use of approved tools only, manager approval and an annual review.

scenes.title: Tiering rules that keep it honest

items.d: EU AI Act high-risk uses are never below tier 3; prohibited uses are never approved

items.h: Tier the use, not the tool
items.d: The same model can be tier 1 in one use and tier 4 in another
New data, users, tools or autonomy mean a new rating
Independent review stops people gaming the questionnaire

scenes.say: A few rules keep tiering honest. | The law sets the floor. A use case that the EU AI Act classes as high risk can never sit below tier three internally, and prohibited practices are never approved. | Tier the use, not the tool. The same model might be tier one for drafting marketing copy and tier four for screening job applicants. | Re-tier on change. New data, new users, new tools or more autonomy mean a new rating. | And check the scoring. A second line reviewer stops teams answering the questionnaire to get the answer they want.

items: Tiers match scrutiny to risk
Human impact × technical complexity
Each tier has defined requirements and approvers
Law sets the floor; tier the use; re-tier on change
scenes.say: To recap. | Risk tiers match the depth of scrutiny to the size of the risk. | Rate each use case on human impact and technical complexity. | Each tier carries defined requirements, approvers and review frequency. | And remember: the law sets the floor, you tier the use rather than the tool, and you re-tier whenever something material changes.

blocks.md:
### Why tier?
Risk tiering applies the principle of **proportionality**: the effort spent on assessment and control should match the risk. Without tiers, organisations either drown low-risk tools in paperwork (driving shadow AI) or wave high-risk systems through. Tiers also make governance **predictable**: teams know in advance what a tier-3 system will need, and can plan for it.

### Building a tiering model
A common approach scores each use case on two dimensions.

**Human impact** (the potential consequences for people):

| Factor | Low (1) | Medium (2) | High (3) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Decisions about people | None | Supports decisions with human review | Makes or heavily shapes significant decisions |
| Safety and critical services | No effect | Indirect effect | Could cause physical harm or disrupt critical services |
| Scale and vulnerability | Few internal users | Many users or customers | Large populations or vulnerable groups |
| Reversibility | Errors trivial to fix | Errors fixable with effort | Errors hard or impossible to undo |
| Data sensitivity | Public or internal | Personal data | Special-category, financial or children’s data |

**Technical complexity** (how hard the system is to predict, control and secure):

| Factor | Low (1) | Medium (2) | High (3) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Autonomy | Suggests only | Acts with approval | Acts autonomously |
| Inputs | Trusted, internal | Mixed | Untrusted external content (web, email, uploads) |
| Integration | Standalone | Reads from systems | Writes to systems or controls other agents |
| Opacity | Interpretable | Partly explainable | Opaque foundation model |
| Dependence | In-house | Established vendor | Novel or opaque third-party components |

The scores combine into a tier, often with **override rules**: any “high” on decisions about people or safety makes the use case at least tier 3, regardless of the total.

### Tier requirements
Each tier specifies:
- **required assessments** (checklist, standard risk assessment, impact assessment, DPIA, bias testing, security testing, red teaming);
- **approval authority** (manager, business owner with second-line sign-off, governance committee, executive acceptance of residual risk);
- **oversight mode** (automated, human on the loop, human in the loop);
- **monitoring and review frequency**;
- **documentation** (inventory entry, model card, decision log).

### External classifications
Internal tiers must respect external rules. Under the **EU AI Act**, prohibited practices map to “not permitted”, high-risk systems to at least tier 3, and limited-risk systems carry mandatory transparency controls whatever their internal tier. Sector rules (financial model-risk guidance, medical device regulation) may add requirements. An internal tier can be **stricter** than the law, but never weaker.

### Common mistakes
- **Tiering the vendor or model instead of the use.** “We approved that model” says nothing about a new, higher-impact use of it.
- **Underestimating generative AI complexity.** A chatbot reading untrusted customer emails with tool access is technically complex, even if building it took a week.
- **Static tiers.** Adding a tool, a data source or more autonomy changes the tier.
- **Self-assessment without challenge.** Second-line review of high-tier and borderline classifications prevents gaming.

blocks.title: Which tier? (using the example model)
pairs: Marketing-copy assistant using approved tools; no personal data
Internal policy Q&A over company documents, read-only
Model that ranks job applicants, with recruiter review
Tier 3: high (at least, as EU AI Act high risk)
Agent that autonomously approves insurance claims and pays out

blocks.title: Proportionality is the point
blocks.md: If a scenario says governance is “slowing everything down” or “being bypassed”, look for an answer that introduces **risk-based tiering**, so low-risk uses move fast and scrutiny concentrates on high-impact ones. If it says a high-risk system “went through the light-touch route”, look for **override rules, re-tiering on change, or second-line review** of the classification.

q.q: A company approved a foundation model for drafting internal newsletters (tier 1). A team now wants to use the same model to make first-round decisions on loan applications. What should happen?
o: Nothing new; the model is already approved, so any team may use it for any purpose
Treat it as a new use case and tier it on its own impact, which will place it in a high tier
Approve it at tier 1, provided each loan decision carries a disclaimer that AI was involved
Ban the model across the organisation, since it has been used for a purpose it wasn’t approved for
q.why: Tiers apply to uses, not tools. Lending decisions have high human impact (and are high risk under the EU AI Act), so the new use needs its own assessment and controls.

blocks.title: Deciding what to do about it

scenes.title: Deciding what to do about it
scenes.sub: Treating AI risks, accepting what remains, and knowing when to look again
scenes.say: Once a risk is understood, someone has to decide what to do about it. And because AI systems change, that decision has a shelf life. | This video covers the four risk treatments, AI-specific examples, residual risk acceptance, and the events that should trigger a fresh assessment.

scenes.title: Four ways to treat a risk

items.d: Don’t do it, or remove the risky capability
Add controls that reduce likelihood or impact
Insurance or contracts; accountability stays with you
Formally retain the risk, within appetite, by an authorised owner

scenes.say: There are four classic treatments. | Avoid: don’t proceed with the use case, or remove the capability that creates the risk, such as an agent’s ability to send external email. | Mitigate: add controls that reduce the likelihood or the impact. This is the most common choice. | Transfer or share: shift some financial consequences through insurance or contract terms, such as a vendor’s indemnity. But accountability to regulators and affected people stays with you. | And accept: formally retain the risk, when it is within appetite, through a documented decision by someone with the authority to make it.

blocks.md:
### Treatment options
ISO 31000 lists several ways to treat risk, which collapse into the four you will see on the exam:

| Treatment | Meaning | AI examples |
|---|---|---|
| **Avoid** | Decide not to start or continue the activity, or remove the source of risk | Don’t deploy emotion recognition for staff evaluation; remove an agent’s ability to execute payments |
| **Mitigate (reduce)** | Change the likelihood or the consequences | Input and output filtering, least-privilege tools, human approval, grounding, bias testing, monitoring, rate limits |
| **Transfer (share)** | Share consequences with another party | Cyber or AI liability insurance; vendor indemnities for IP claims; contractual SLAs with service credits |
| **Accept (retain)** | Knowingly retain the risk within appetite | Accept residual hallucination risk for an internal drafting tool with human review |

Two cautions on **transfer**. First, insurance and contracts move *financial* consequences, not **accountability**: regulators, courts and customers still hold the organisation responsible. Second, insurance policies may exclude or limit AI-related losses, so check coverage explicitly.

### Choosing mitigations
Good mitigations are **specific** to the risk scenario, **layered** (defence in depth), and **verified** (tested to show they work). For AI they often combine:
- **preventive controls** (access restrictions, input isolation, approval gates);
- **detective controls** (monitoring, anomaly detection, audit logging);
- **corrective controls** (rollback, kill switches, incident playbooks);
- **directive controls** (policies, training, acceptable use).

Cost matters. Use the safeguard value formula from Section 1: **ALE before − ALE after − annual cost of the control**. A control that costs more than the loss it prevents is hard to justify, unless law, safety or ethics requires it.

### Residual risk and formal acceptance
After treatment, **residual risk** remains. Accepting it is a governance act, not a default:
- the acceptor must have **authority** proportionate to the level of risk (set out in the risk appetite statement);
- acceptance is **documented**, with the rationale, conditions and compensating controls;
- it is **time-bound**, with a review date, and recorded in an exception or risk-acceptance register;
- it is **revisited** when triggers fire.

Risk can’t be accepted beyond legal limits: you can’t “accept” operating a prohibited AI practice.

### Reassessment triggers
| Trigger | Examples | Typical response |
|---|---|---|
| **Model updates** | Retraining, fine-tuning, provider version change, new system prompt | Regression and safety tests; scoped reassessment |
| **Behavioural or performance drift** | Accuracy, fairness or refusal rates cross thresholds | Investigate cause; retrain, recalibrate or roll back |
| **Vulnerability disclosures** | New jailbreak technique, CVE in an inference server, poisoned public dataset | Assess exposure using the inventory and AIBOM; patch or apply compensating controls |
| **Incidents and near misses** | Your own or a peer organisation’s | Root cause analysis; update controls and assessments |
| **Change in scope** | New users, purpose, data, tools, integrations or autonomy | Re-tier; reassess impact and blast radius |
| **External change** | New regulation or guidance; vendor terms or ownership change | Gap assessment against new requirements |
| **Time** | Scheduled review by tier | Confirm assessment still valid |

The reassessment should be **proportionate**: a minor change gets a quick check, a major change a full reassessment. What matters is that triggers are **defined in advance, owned, and connected** to the processes that detect them (change management, model registry, monitoring, threat intelligence and vendor management).

blocks.title: The quiet model update
blocks.md: A hosted model provider announces that its “latest” model alias now points to a new version with improved reasoning. An insurer’s claims assistant uses that alias. The assistant’s risk assessment was completed nine months ago, and its next scheduled review is in three months.

o: Wait for the scheduled review in three months, since the risk assessment is still within its validity period
Treat the change as a trigger: pin the old version if possible, test the new one, and reassess before switching
Accept the update automatically, since the provider has tested it and says the new version performs better
Switch to a different provider whose model aliases never change, and repeat the procurement process
q.why: A model version change is a standard reassessment trigger. Pinning, testing and a scoped reassessment let the insurer adopt the improvement safely. Waiting or accepting blindly leaves unknown behaviour changes in a system that affects customers.

q.q: An organisation buys insurance to cover losses from AI-related errors. Which statement is MOST accurate?
o: The organisation is no longer accountable for the outcomes, because the insurer now carries that risk
Insurance shifts some financial consequences, but legal and regulatory accountability stay with the organisation
Insurance removes the need for other controls, provided the policy covers the full value of potential losses
Insurance is a form of risk avoidance, because it stops AI-related losses from reaching the organisation
q.why: Risk transfer shares financial impact; it never transfers accountability to regulators, customers or affected people, and it doesn’t replace mitigation.

quiz.q: Which formula gives the annualised loss expectancy (ALE)?
o: ALE = AV × ARO
ALE = SLE × ARO
ALE = SLE ÷ EF
ALE = AV + SLE
quiz.why: ALE is the single loss expectancy multiplied by the annualised rate of occurrence. SLE itself is asset value × exposure factor.

quiz.q: What is the difference between inherent and residual risk?
o: Inherent risk is financial in nature, while residual risk is reputational
Inherent risk is before controls; residual risk is what remains after controls
Inherent risk applies only to AI systems, while residual risk applies to all IT
They describe the same risk, measured by different teams at different times
quiz.why: Inherent risk ignores controls; residual risk is the exposure left once controls operate. Residual risk is never zero.

quiz.q: Which model quantifies risk by decomposing it into loss event frequency and loss magnitude?
o: STRIDE
FAIR
RACI
MITRE ATLAS
quiz.why: FAIR (Factor Analysis of Information Risk) is a quantitative model built on loss event frequency and loss magnitude, often estimated as ranges.

quiz.q: Which assessment does the EU AI Act require of certain deployers, such as those assessing creditworthiness, before using high-risk AI?
o: An independent penetration test
A fundamental rights impact assessment
A business continuity and recovery plan
A software bill of materials (SBOM)
quiz.why: Article 27 requires a FRIA from public bodies, private entities providing public services, and deployers of credit-scoring and certain insurance systems.

quiz.q: What determines an AI system’s blast radius?
o: Its intended purpose, as described in the approved design document and policy
The data, actions and connections it can actually reach, and the scale it operates at
The size of its underlying model in parameters, which sets how much it can do
The number of developers who built it and the number of teams who maintain it
quiz.why: Blast radius depends on permissions and integrations. A system intended for a narrow task but given broad access has a broad blast radius.

quiz.q: Which two dimensions are commonly combined to tier AI use cases?
o: Cost and speed
Human impact and technical complexity
Model size and vendor
Number of users and colour of the interface
quiz.why: Human impact captures potential harm to people; technical complexity captures how hard the system is to predict, control and secure.

quiz.q: A model approved for a low-risk use is proposed for a high-impact use. What is the correct approach?
o: Reuse the original approval, as long as the model version hasn’t changed
Tier and assess the new use case on its own impact and its complexity
Approve it, since the model has already passed a full risk assessment
Reject all future uses of the model to keep the approval process simple
quiz.why: Risk attaches to the use, not the tool. A new purpose, population or decision type needs its own tier and assessment.

quiz.q: Buying insurance to cover losses from AI errors is an example of which treatment?
o: Avoidance (termination)
Mitigation (reduction)
Transfer (risk sharing)
Acceptance (retention)
quiz.why: Insurance shares financial consequences with another party. Accountability to regulators and affected people remains with the organisation.

quiz.q: Removing an agent’s ability to execute payments, because the risk is too high, is an example of:
o: Risk avoidance
Risk transfer
Risk acceptance
Risk tolerance
quiz.why: Removing the capability that creates the risk avoids it. Adding approval steps instead would be mitigation.

quiz.q: Which event should MOST clearly trigger a reassessment of a deployed AI system?
o: A routine backup of the system’s configuration and logs completing
The provider replacing the model version behind the API
The development team moving to a new office in another city
A change to the application’s colour theme and branding
quiz.why: Model changes can alter behaviour, including safety and fairness, so they are a standard reassessment trigger.

exam.q: An AI-enabled fraud scenario has an SLE of £250,000 and an ARO of 0.4. A control costing £40,000 a year would reduce the ARO to 0.1. What is the annual value of the control?
exam.why: ALE before = £250,000 × 0.4 = £100,000. ALE after = £250,000 × 0.1 = £25,000. Reduction = £75,000. Minus the £40,000 cost, the control is worth £35,000 a year.

exam.q: In an AI risk workshop, almost every risk is rated “medium” on a three-point scale, and the board cannot prioritise. What is the BEST improvement?
o: Rate every uncertain risk as high, so that the board treats all of them as priorities for funding
Define clear likelihood and impact criteria, including impact on people, and map risks to components and owners
Replace the three-point scale with a ten-point scale so that small differences between risks can be shown
Ask each risk owner to re-rate their own risks without the workshop, to avoid groupthink in the room
exam.why: Vague scales produce undifferentiated ratings. Defined criteria, quantification where possible, and mapping to components and owners make prioritisation and action possible.

exam.q: An EU bank will deploy a high-risk creditworthiness model and already has a GDPR DPIA for it. What is the MOST efficient way to meet the fundamental rights impact assessment duty?
o: Skip the FRIA, since the GDPR DPIA already covers every risk to fundamental rights that the AI Act requires of deployers
Build the FRIA on the DPIA, adding affected groups, rights risks, oversight and responses, then notify the authority
Commission a separate team to start the FRIA from scratch, so that it is independent of the privacy work
Ask the model provider to complete the FRIA, since the provider designed the system and knows its risks
exam.why: The AI Act lets a FRIA build on a DPIA, but it must still address fundamental rights beyond data protection, and the deployer must notify the authority. The duty belongs to the deployer, not the provider.

exam.q: An impact assessment finds that an email-handling agent with a broad service account has a very large blast radius. Which treatment is MOST effective?
o: Add a sentence to the system prompt asking the agent to take great care with high-impact actions
Reduce permissions to least privilege, segment access, and add limits and approval for high-impact actions
Increase the agent’s context window so that it can see the full history before acting on any email
Monitor the agent’s actions every week, and quickly roll back any harmful changes that the security review identifies
exam.why: Blast radius shrinks only when reach shrinks. Least privilege, segmentation, limits and approvals reduce both likelihood and impact; prompts don’t enforce, and weekly review is too slow.

exam.q: Teams are bypassing AI governance because every request, however small, requires a 40-page assessment. What is the BEST fix?
o: Enforce the 40-page assessment more strictly, with sanctions for teams that skip it
Introduce risk-based tiers with proportionate requirements, and second-line review of tiers
Stop assessing low-value AI use cases altogether and focus only on externally facing systems
Let each team decide for itself whether governance applies to its particular use of AI
exam.why: Proportionate tiering lets low-risk uses move quickly and concentrates effort on high-impact ones, removing the incentive to bypass governance. Review of classifications prevents gaming.

exam.q: Threat intelligence reports a new indirect prompt injection technique affecting RAG applications built on a particular open-source framework. What should the risk owner do FIRST?
o: Wait for the next scheduled review of each affected system, when the new technique can be considered properly and in full
Use the inventory and AIBOM to find affected systems, triage the change in risk, and reassess or add controls
Shut down every AI system in the organisation until the framework’s maintainers release a patch
Ask each development team to confirm whether they use the framework, and record their answers
exam.why: A vulnerability disclosure is a reassessment trigger. Identifying exposure and triaging comes first, then a proportionate response; blanket shutdowns or waiting are disproportionate either way.
